Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are set to debate Tuesday, the first time voters will see them share a stage.

Democrats have long coveted Collins’ seat, which she has held since 1996. But she’s never faced a reelection battle quite like this. The opponent Democratic voters nominated in June, Graham Platner, abruptly withdrew from the race after a woman credibly accused him of sexual assault. (Platner has denied the allegation.) Jackson was nominated to replace Platner at a convention later that month.

Most polls show Jackson ahead of Collins, but the incumbent is outspending him on the airwaves. Tonight’s debate is certain to feature talk about the cost of living, the Iran War, President Donald Trump and Collins’ recent spate of negative national press. Follow along with us live here.

Not to get too pundit-y here, but I am not sure this debate changed much.

It was a classic Collins performance. She demonstrated a firm grasp of the business of Washington. Jackson spoke well, and hammered his campaign’s key points of criticism of Collins. In some ways, it was a distillation of the past few weeks of campaigning.

But I didn’t see anything game changing. Three more debates to go!

-Kirby Wilson

The debate ended on a friendly note, with Jackson and Collins making their pitches to voters.

Collins alluded yet again to the money she has won for Maine and highlighted the Social Security Fairness Act she helped author and that became law. She said she opposed both Biden and Trump at times.

“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation,” Collins said.

Jackson said that “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. You know, I owe the people of the state everything.” He brought up again how Collins voted with Trump around 96% of the time and that she’s been fighting for “the billionaire class.”

“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is, but power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people in Maine need it,” Jackson said, adding he passed legislation at the State House to lower prescription drug costs, support childcare and provide universal school meals along with sponsoring abortion access legislation.

“I’m never going to forget where I came from. I’m an everyday person that is so indebted to people who put me in this position to fight for them,” Jackson said.

The two shared a laugh when moderator Gregg Lagerquist of WGME said at the end he was going to ask both of them during the lightning round if the New England Patriots will make the playoffs.

Collins said they absolutely will, and razzed Jackson for being a Steelers fan.

Each candidate left the stage smiling.

-Kirby Wilson

When asked a series of lightning round questions, the candidates agreed on the following:

-There should be more AI guardrails

-There should be more restrictions on data centers

-Mifepristone, which is a medication used for abortions, should be available.
